title: Understanding Squeezed States of Light Through Wigner's Phase-Space
abstract: This paper starts with the transition from classical physics to quantum mechanics which was greatly aided by the concept of phase space. The role of canonical transformations in quantum mechanics is addressed. The Wigner phase-space distribution function is then defined which arises from the formulation of the density matrix, followed by the harmonic oscillator in phase space. Coherent and one- and two-mode squeezed states of light as well as the squeezed vacuum are discussed in the phase-space picture. Attention is also drawn to the fact that squeezed states naturally generate entanglement between the two-modes. Coupled harmonic oscillators are also elucidated in connection with the Wigner phase space. It will be noted that the phase-space picture of quantum mechanics has become an important scientific language for the rapidly expanding field of quantum optics. Here, we mainly focus on the simplest form of the Wigner function, which finds application in many branches of quantum mechanics. We make use of several symmetry groups such as Lorentz groups, the symplectic group in two and four dimensions, and the Euclidean group. The decoherence problem of an optical field is examined through a reformulation of the Poincaré sphere as a further illustration of the density matrix.
summary: This paper develops an advanced theoretical framework using the Wigner phase-space distribution function to analyze squeezed states of light. It unifies concepts from classical mechanics, quantum optics, and group theory by showing that state transformations are governed by specific symmetry groups like the symplectic or Lorentz groups. This provides a powerful mathematical tool for understanding entanglement and decoherence in quantum optical systems.
main_problem: The paper aims to elucidate squeezed states of light using a unified framework based on quantum phase space, canonical transformations, and group theory.
main_result: Phase space provides a powerful, symmetry-preserving language for quantum optics, showing that coherent and squeezed states can be generated from the vacuum via canonical transformations corresponding to specific Lie groups (like $	ext{Sp}(2)$ or Lorentz/symplectic groups).
method: The analysis heavily relies on defining and manipulating the Wigner phase-space distribution function, connecting it to density matrices, and employing group theoretical methods involving symplectic and Lorentz symmetries.
model_or_system: The primary system is light fields modeled by quantized harmonic oscillators. The mathematical framework extends from 2D (single mode) to 4D (two modes), incorporating concepts like the Poincaré sphere for polarization description.
key_observables: Wigner function $W(x, p)$, squeezing parameters ($\lambda$), entanglement measures, and expectation values derived from phase-space integrals.
important_parameters: The analysis uses natural units ($\hbar=c=1$) and focuses on the structure imposed by various symmetry groups (Lorentz, symplectic $	ext{Sp}(2n)$).
main_assumptions: The focus is primarily on the simplest form of the Wigner function; mathematical derivations often rely on established group theory results.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate squeezing via transformation from a circle to an ellipse while preserving area, show time evolution of Gaussian wave packets (shear), and compare Wigner functions for different excitation levels ($n=0, 1, 2, 3$), highlighting negativity in excited states.
paper_structure: The paper progresses by establishing the phase-space formalism ($	ext{Wigner} 	o 	ext{Density Matrix}$), detailing canonical transformations and associated symmetry groups (Euclidean/Symplectic), applying this to simple systems (harmonic oscillator, free particles), extending to multi-mode systems (two-mode squeezing), and finally relating symmetries to polarization optics via the Poincaré sphere.
why_interesting: This work is highly relevant as it provides a deep mathematical underpinning for quantum optics by unifying state descriptions (Wigner function) with fundamental symmetry principles (Lie groups), which is crucial for understanding complex light-matter interactions.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Illustrated as a blue circle, it corresponds to the initial vacuum state in phase space, whose area is proportional to and is a representative of minimum uncertainty ∆x∆p = 1/4. When the circle is squeezed, it is transformed into an ellipse, shown in red. This has the same area as the circle and thus is also a representative of minimum uncertainty.

Figure 2: The transformations of Sp(2) produce rotations and squeezes. The circle in this figure corresponds to a Gaussian distribution. As shown on the left, the Lorentz boost of SO(2 , 1) along the z-direction corresponds to the squeeze of Sp(2) along the x-axis of the phase space. On the right is the action of the rotated squeeze of Sp(2), which transforms the circle into a tilted ellipse whose major axis is aligned along the p = x line. This transformation corresponds to the boost along the x-direction of SO(2 , 1).
Figure 3: The spread of the Gaussian wave packet. The circle represents the Gaussian distribution, while the tilted ellipse represents the time development [68].

Figure 4: Wigner functions (with right-angle cross sections) of the harmonic oscillator for the ground state and for the first three excited states. The symmetry of the Wigner function with respect to x and p is apparent. It can also be observed that higher the excited state the function has more ripples around the origin.

Figure 5: The Wigner function for the harmonic oscillator in the first excited state. It is negative at the origin, becomes positive as (x2 + p2) increases, and becomes vanishingly small as (x2 + p2) becomes very large. If this Wigner function is integrated over p, then it becomes the quantum probability distribution in x, which is ρ1(x) = 2x2e−x2/√π, and is positive for all values of x.
